newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - UK growth set to accelerate in 1997 - analysts.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - UK growth set to accelerate in 1997 - analysts.

text.p: Britain's pace of economic growth quickened in the third quarter and looks set to accelerate next year, official figures published on Friday showed.
Gross Domestic Product rose by 2.3 percent in the third quarter from 2.2 percent in the second, suggesting the economy is enjoying more lively growth without igniting inflation.
British finance minister Kenneth Clarke hailed the figures and said: "The UK is well on course to growth faster than France and Germany for the fourth successive year."
The data pointed to more balanced economic growth with manufacturing output starting to pick-up, bolstering strong growth in the service sector.
They will give a welcome boost to the ruling Conservative party, which wants to keep the economy on an even keel of steady growth and low inflation ahead of the general election.

The government, which is trailing the opposition Labour party by 14 points according to the latest poll, is hoping growing consumer confidence will give them the lift they need between now and May 1997, the deadline for holding the election.
Friday's data are the last on the economy ahead of the Chancellor's regular monetary policy meeting with Bank of England governor Eddie George next Wednesday.
Economists said Clarke would use the figures to resist calls by the governor for a rise in UK interest rates.

"The figures show although the economy is growing at a strong pace there is no hint of a boom. They should give Clarke enough leeway to leave rates on hold next week," said Andrew Cates, UK economist at UBS.

Clarke has cut interest rates four times since last December to their present 5.75 percent level and is under considerable political pressure to resist calls for a further increase before the election.

Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic advisor at Bank America, agreed the Chancellor would use the GDP figures to argue for rates on hold. "The rise in GDP should constitute the final nail in the coffin of rate cut hopes, but it will certainly not be deemed strong enough by Clarke to justify a tightening."
The steady rise in GDP dispells any notion that growth is out of control and a 1980s type boom is brewing.

In an interview with Britain's Evening Standard published on Friday, Clarke said: "The recovery...is strengthening as the year is going on. It's combined with low inflation in a way that's never been achieved in previous British recoveries in my adult life."

Other figures released on Friday showed the trade gap between Britain and the rest of the world improved dramatically in August, narrowing to 584 million sterling ($929.1 million) from 1.22 billion in July.
More up-to-date but incomplete trade figures showed exports to countries outside the EU dropped slightly in September, with the trade gap widening to 851 million sterling from 597 million in August.
Economists said it was too early to tell whether the recent rise in sterling was choking exports by making them more expensive.

"It's always difficult to work out how much is to do with appreciation and how much to do with weakness overseas. I think in this case it's more to do with slower growth overseas," especially in the U.S.," said Bank America's Jeremy Hawkins.
